report.answer_text:
Yes, in most places you can. Many police departments, sheriff's offices, and some other agencies run civilian ride-along programs. Each agency sets its own rules, so the details vary.
Common requirements
Age: Usually 18 or older. Some agencies allow younger teens with a parent's or guardian's consent.
Background check: Most agencies run one and turn you down if you have a serious criminal record or active warrants.
Application and waiver: You fill out a form and sign a liability waiver.
ID: You bring a valid government-issued ID.
Dress code: Business casual is typical. Some agencies ban offensive clothing or open-toed shoes.
Residency: Some agencies only accept residents or people with a connection to the community, such as students, journalists, or those interested in a law enforcement career.
How to set one up
1. Look on the website of your local police department or sheriff's office and search for "ride-along."
2. If you can't find it, call the non-emergency line or the community relations or public information office.
3. Submit the application. Approval can take days to weeks.
4. Expect a shift of about 4 to 8 hours. Some agencies have a waiting list or limit how often you can ride.
What to expect
You'll ride in the front or back seat and follow the officer's instructions.
Officers may tell you to stay in the car during certain calls.
You may see stressful or disturbing situations.
Agencies often limit what you can record or share, especially anything involving victims or suspects.
Some agencies don't offer ride-alongs at all, or have paused them because of staffing, insurance, or policy changes.
If you tell me your city or county, I can look up the specific program and application process. Federal agencies like the FBI generally don't offer ride-alongs to the public.
